description: Eight scripted multi-turn conversations, from a user's first message to the end of a search. Each turn carries its own expectations, so any model or agent can be scored on the whole journey rather than on one finished report. Facts come only from the attachments a turn pastes in, or from the legal facts in the skill; every expectation is checkable by keyword, regex or numeric extraction.

grading.turn_score: passed checks / checks that applied on that turn
grading.journey_score: the mean of the turn scores
grading.completed: true when every turn produced a non-empty reply
grading.facts: Every number a turn expects is extracted from the reply by that fact's own regexes and compared with the value taken from the attachment (or computed from it with the formula in `why`). A number of the same kind that is not the expected one is counted as a fabrication. A fact the reply never states is `skipped` unless it is marked `required`.
grading.tone: A blocklist of disrespectful phrases in English and Chinese, held in bench/journeys.py as TONE_BLOCKLIST, is applied to every reply. 'Roast' means candid, specific, evidence-based criticism of the LISTING under its landmine code. Insults or accusations about landlords, agents or hosts fail the turn outright.
grading.questions: max_questions counts '?' and '？' after masking quoted spans, so a question written FOR the user to send to an agent does not count against the agent's own question budget.
grading.judge_notes: Per turn and per journey, for an optional model judge. Nothing reads them for the score.

glossary.roast: The candid, specific, evidence-based critique of a listing or a building: every criticism carries the landmine code and the line on the page that earned it. In Chinese the word is 尻洗（台語，roast）- Taiwanese Hokkien, and it marks the author's origin. Both words mean the same thing and either may appear in a user turn or in a reply; the checks accept both.
glossary.what_roast_is_not: Not an insult and not an accusation about a person. Landlords, agents and hosts are partners in the search. Roast the listing, never the person - 尻洗房源，不尻洗人。 TONE_BLOCKLIST in bench/journeys.py enforces it on every reply.

fictional_data.notice: Every address, postcode, building, company and person in this file is invented. The postcodes all begin with X, a letter the United Kingdom never uses to start a postcode area, so none of them can collide with a real address. The runner tells the agent under test that the material is fictional test data and should be treated as real for the exercise.

check_grammar.must: a list of items. A plain string is a case-insensitive substring. An object takes `label` plus exactly one of `any_of` (one of these substrings is present), `all_of` (all of them are), or `regex` (a Python regex that matches).
check_grammar.must_not: the same grammar; the item fails the turn when it MATCHES.
check_grammar.facts: name -> {value | values, tolerance, required, patterns, near, window, mask_patterns, source, why}. Group 1 of each pattern is the number.
check_grammar.max_questions: an integer ceiling on '?' plus '？' in the reply, quoted spans masked out.
check_grammar.ends_with: a string, or {any_of: [...]}, that must appear in the last `ends_within` characters (default 300).
check_grammar.language: 'en' or a zh tag; checked by the share of CJK characters in the reply.
check_grammar.workdir_expect: file path -> {contains: [...], absent: [...]} (a plain list means contains). Checked in the run's own folder after the turn, so 'applied' is graded on the file, not on the words. Skipped for the api agent, which has no folder. An attachment with a `file` key is written into the folder before its turn, title line dropped.

journeys.title: 從零開始 — from nothing to a first candidate
persona: Wei, 23, a Taiwanese postgraduate who starts a London master's in October and has rented only in Taipei; has never seen a UK tenancy, an energy certificate or a referencing check.

Chat box on a phone: no shell, no fetcher, no browser add-on, so everything the agent needs must be pasted in by hand. Knowledge level: beginner - does not know what a holding deposit or a guarantor is.
journeys.outcome: The user arrives knowing nothing and leaves with: the ten basics stated with the correct legal caps, a profile written back to her in plain words with every default named, a manual-mode paste list given once, one candidate held under two gate questions, and a next-step checklist. Nothing about any flat is asserted that she did not paste.
journeys.judge_notes: Does it read as one person talking to a frightened beginner, or as a form? Are the defaults sensible for London in October rather than arbitrary? Does it keep moving - proposing the next step itself instead of waiting to be asked? Does it stay warm about the agent and landlord she will have to deal with?

journeys.title: 這個房源幫我尻洗 — one listing, one certificate, one gate
persona: Chen, 26, a Taiwanese design student already in London on a two-week hotel booking; she has found one flat she likes and wants a second opinion before she pays anything.
Chat box only: she copies pages out of the browser and pastes them. Reads English fine but wants the verdict in Chinese. Knowledge level: has read a bit, believes the advertised square footage.
journeys.outcome: A verdict built only on the two pages she pasted: 48 m² from the certificate against 592 sq ft advertised (the balcony), first assessment 2019, a communal heat network with no tariff, and three money terms above the legal caps. Two killer questions from the bank, the viewing-day checks, and when the agent answers 'UK guarantor only' the G1 gate is applied politely rather than argued with.
journeys.judge_notes: Does every number in the verdict trace to one of the two pasted pages? Is the area illusion explained so a beginner sees it, rather than asserted? When the gate closes, does the reply keep the door open with the agent instead of blaming them?

journeys.title: Roast my short stays / 幫我尻洗這幾間短租 - four bridges, one arithmetic
persona: Tom, 31, lands on Sunday and needs 30 nights while he house-hunts; he has booked short lets before and thinks he can spot a bad one from the photographs.
Chat box only, on a phone at the airport, so everything is pasted. Knowledge level: confident but wrong about total price; has asked in so many words for blunt criticism.
